newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam makes room for currency to slip.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam makes room for currency to slip.

text.p: Vietnam has widened the official exchange fluctuation band for its currency, the dong, leaving room for market pressure to take it lower against the U.S. dollar, bankers said on Monday.

There was no announcement of the move from the central State Bank of Vietnam, which has recently been at pains to scotch speculation that a devaluation was being considered as a solution to the communist country's balloning trade deficit.
Bankers in Hanoi said the dong's fluctuation band, outside which they are not allowed to deal, had been widened to plus/minus one percent from plus/minus 0.5 percent.
The new band will, like the previous one, have 11,030 per dollar as its pivot rate, with the upper end at 10,920 and the lower end at 11,140.
The dong, which has been steady at around 11,000 per dollar since 1994, nudged down briefly to below its old lower limit of 11,085 after the news came out on Monday, but trade was very thin.
"People are being a bit wary for the moment," said one dealer at a bank in Hanoi, who declined to be named. "But as soon as anyone needs dollars, the rate is going to go up."

"There has been a lot of pressure in the market to buy dollars, but until now we have been stuck at the limit of the previous band and the market was starting to stagnate," said Peter McLean at Standard Chartered Bank. "This frees it up."

He said that with import customers of the banking community looking to buy dollars at the moment, there was a risk that the dong would slip quickly to its new lower limit of 11,140 and get stuck again.
With imports flooding the economy authorities have been considering a depreciation as a way to make imports more expensive and exports cheaper.
The government has forecast a record trade deficit of $4.0 billion for this year compared with $2.3 billion in 1995.
However, bankers pointed out that the government has worked for years to promote confidence in the dong and would be most unlikely to put that at risk by sanctioning a sudden drop in its value.
"This has been a fairly bold move for Vietnam and I wouldn't see further widening (of the fluctuation band) in the near term," said one.
He said it was possible the central bank would sell dollars in coming days to ensure a smooth trnasition to the trading range.
